I have been working this land for fifty years. I know what this soil needs and what it will give back. My back is not as strong as it used to be, and my sons are mostly in the city, so I cannot do everything myself. But I know the rhythm of this land — wheat goes in after the maize comes off, maize goes in right after wheat harvest, and cotton takes the other plots from spring through picking season in October.

I split my 13.1 mu like this: 8 mu I run in the wheat-maize double-crop rotation, the way I have done for thirty years. The other 5.1 mu I put in cotton. Cotton is hard on my body at harvest time, but the price is still better than just grain, and I know how to grow it. I will hire a day laborer or two for cotton picking if I need to.

For wheat, I buy the improved variety seed from the township cooperative — Kenong or Jimai, whichever they have. I do not experiment with new things at my age. I apply base fertilizer at planting and topdress at jointing. I irrigate three times: once before winter sets in to protect the roots, once at jointing, once at heading. Two spray rounds for rust and weeds. I use rotary tillage after maize harvest to work the stubble in.

For summer maize, I use hybrid seed — Zhengdan 958 or something close to it. I have used it for years. Right after wheat harvest I plant with no tillage, because there is no time to waste and the soil is fine. I irrigate twice, at planting and at silking. I spray once for corn borer and once for weeds.

For cotton, I plough in spring and apply a full base fertilizer. Cotton takes a lot of water at flowering and boll setting, so I irrigate five times from the well. I spray five or six times across the season — aphids come every year without fail.

I do not change my methods much. What has worked for fifty years I trust more than what any pamphlet says.
